El Niño Outlook ( September 2026 - March 2027 )

Last Updated: 9 September 2026
( Next update will be on 9 October 2026 )


    • El Niño conditions are considered to have persisted in the equatorial Pacific since Spring 2026.
    • They are virtually certain (100%) to continue until boreal winter.

[El Niño / La Niña]

In August 2026, the sea surface temperature (SST) for the NINO.3 region was above normal with a deviation of +3.4°C. The value exceeded the previous August record of +3.0°C observed in 1997, the highest August value since 1949 (Fig.3 and Table). The five-month running mean value of the NINO.3 SST deviation for June 2026 was +1.9°C, remaining above the threshold for the third consecutive month (Fig.1 and Table). SSTs in the equatorial Pacific were above normal in the central and eastern parts and below normal in the western part (Fig.4 and Fig.6). Subsurface water temperatures in the equatorial Pacific were above normal in the central and eastern parts, and below normal in the western part (Fig.5 and Fig.7). In the atmosphere, convective activity was enhanced in the vicinity of the equatorial dateline, and easterly winds in the lower troposphere (i.e., trade winds) over the central equatorial Pacific were significantly weaker than normal (Fig.8, Fig.9 and Fig.10). These oceanic and atmospheric conditions indicate that El Niño features have been steadily strengthening since the spring of 2026. From the above, it is concluded that El Niño conditions are considered to have persisted since Spring 2026.

The warm subsurface water in the central and eastern parts of equatorial Pacific has maintained warm SST in NINO.3 region. JMA's seasonal ensemble prediction system predicts that the subsurface water in the central and eastern parts will rise due to atmosphere-ocean interaction. As a result, the NINO.3 SST is expected to increase until boreal winter, and the El Niño event is likely to peak during the season. Accordingly, the SST anomaly is expected to reach a level comparable to +3.6°C recorded in December 1997, the highest peak value on record for an El Niño event (Fig.11). In conclusion, El Niño conditions are virtually certain (100%) to continue until boreal winter.

[Western Pacific and Indian Ocean]

The area-averaged SST in the tropical western Pacific (NINO.WEST) region was below normal in August (Fig.3). The index is likely to be below normal until boreal winter (Fig.12).

The area-averaged SST in the tropical Indian Ocean (IOBW) region was near normal in August (Fig.3). The IOBW index is likely to be above normal until boreal winter (Fig.13). The Indian Ocean Dipole Mode Index (DMI) was +0.35 (Fig.3 and Fig.4).

[Impacts]

The following weather conditions observed in August were consistent with those in the months of August during the past El Niño events.

- Above normal temperatures from Kalimantan to southern South Asia, in West Africa, and across the tropical regions from South America through Central America to the central Pacific.

- Below normal temperatures were in the southwestern Polynesia.

- Above normal precipitation from southern Peru to central Chile.

- Below normal precipitation over northern South America and surrounding areas, and southern Southeast Asia.
